description: Prepare and deliver a hard conversation using the three-conversations model from Stone, Patton, and Heen. Separate what happened from feelings from identity, lead with curiosity, state impact without attributing intent, and propose next steps. Works for performance issues, a strained partnership, or any conversation you have been avoiding.

steps.description: Every hard conversation is three tangled conversations at once: what happened, the feelings involved, and the identity at stake. Pull them apart before you plan anything, because a sentence that mixes all three lands as an attack.

inputs.name: conversation-situation
inputs.desc: What the conversation is about and what you have been avoiding saying

inputs.name: other-party-context
inputs.desc: Who the other person is, your relationship, and what you know about their view

outputs.name: what-happened-conversation
outputs.desc: The facts, the differing stories about them, and where you each assign blame

outputs.name: feelings-conversation
outputs.desc: The emotions present for you and likely present for them, named rather than acted out

outputs.name: identity-conversation
outputs.desc: What this situation says to each of you about who you are, the quiet threat underneath

process: Write the situation out once in full, then tag each sentence as a fact claim, a feeling, or an identity statement. Most sentences will be a blend. Split them.
For the what-happened strand, list the objective facts separately from each side's story about those facts. Two people can agree on the facts and still tell opposite stories.
For the feelings strand, name the emotions on both sides. Do not decide yet whether they are justified. Naming is not agreeing.
For the identity strand, finish the sentence 'If this is true, it means I am ...' for yourself and guess the same for them. That ending is the real stake.

steps.description: Move the what-happened strand from blame to contribution. Blame asks who is at fault and ends the conversation. Contribution asks how each person added to the situation and keeps it open. Replace certainty about their intent with curiosity about their view.

inputs.name: what-happened-conversation
inputs.desc: The facts, stories, and blame from the situation

inputs.name: other-party-context
inputs.desc: What you know about the other person's perspective

outputs.name: contribution-map
outputs.desc: How each person, including you, contributed to the situation, stated without fault language

outputs.name: curiosity-questions
outputs.desc: Open questions that invite the other person's story instead of asserting your own

process: For each part of the situation, write one line on how you contributed, even if their share is larger. A conversation where only one side contributed is almost always a story, not a fact.
Write one line on how they contributed, describing the action and its effect, not the motive you assumed.
Convert each assumption about their intent into a question. 'You did not care about the deadline' becomes 'What was going on for you as the deadline approached?'
Keep only questions you would genuinely want answered. A question you already know the answer to is a trap, and the other person will feel it.

steps.description: Plan how to handle the feelings strand. Feelings are to be acknowledged, not debated. When someone feels unheard, no amount of logic moves them. Acknowledgment is not agreement, it is proof you understood.

inputs.name: feelings-conversation
inputs.desc: The emotions present on both sides

inputs.name: contribution-map
inputs.desc: How each side contributed, which often explains the feelings

outputs.name: feelings-inventory
outputs.desc: The feelings you will name openly and the ones you will hold back for now

outputs.name: acknowledgment-statements
outputs.desc: Sentences that show you understood their feeling without conceding the facts

process: List your own feelings and decide which to state directly. Some belong in the conversation, some belong in your own preparation only.

For each feeling you expect from them, write an acknowledgment sentence of the form 'It makes sense you would feel X given Y.' This names the feeling and its cause without ruling on whether the facts support it.
Separate acknowledgment from agreement in your own notes, so that under pressure you do not slide from 'I hear that you are frustrated' into 'you are right to be frustrated' before you mean to.
Decide what you will do if feelings escalate: name the escalation out loud, slow down, and return to acknowledgment before continuing.

steps.description: Name the identity threat under the conversation for both of you. Hard conversations feel hard because they threaten how we see ourselves: as competent, as good, as worthy. Ground yourself before the conversation so a single comment does not knock you off balance.

inputs.name: identity-conversation
inputs.desc: What the situation says to each of you about who you are

inputs.name: feelings-inventory
inputs.desc: The feelings you plan to name, which often trace back to identity

outputs.name: identity-threats
outputs.desc: The specific self-image each person is defending, for you and for them

outputs.name: grounding-reframes
outputs.desc: Reframes that let you hold the threat without collapsing or counterattacking

process: Name your own identity threat in one sentence: the thing you are afraid this conversation proves about you.

Replace the all-or-nothing version with a complex one. 'I am either a good manager or a failure' becomes 'I am a capable manager who handled this part poorly.' Black-and-white identities shatter under pressure.
Guess their identity threat and plan to avoid stepping on it. If they fear looking incompetent, lead with contribution and curiosity, not with a verdict.
Write one grounding line to say to yourself if you feel the threat spike mid-conversation, so you can stay present instead of defending.

steps.description: State the impact of what happened without attributing intent. You can know the impact on you with certainty. You cannot know their intent. Confusing the two turns a describable harm into an accusation they will deny.

inputs.name: contribution-map
inputs.desc: How each side contributed to the situation

inputs.name: feelings-inventory
inputs.desc: The feelings that the impact produced in you

outputs.name: impact-statements
outputs.desc: Sentences describing the effect on you, separated from any claim about why they acted

outputs.name: intent-separation-notes
outputs.desc: The intent claims you removed and why each one would derail the conversation

process: Write the impact as 'When X happened, the effect on me was Y.' Keep Y to observable consequences and named feelings.
Strike every clause that asserts their intent. 'You ignored me to make me look bad' claims a motive. 'When I did not hear back, I was left unsure where the project stood' states the impact.
Where you suspect intent, convert it into a curiosity question for later, not a statement now.
Read each impact statement aloud and check it against one test: could they agree this was the effect, even while disagreeing about why? If not, it still contains a hidden accusation.

steps.description: Assemble the conversation: a curiosity-led opening, the acknowledgment and impact in the middle, and a concrete proposal for next steps. The opening sets the frame, and a frame of joint problem-solving beats a frame of verdict-delivery every time.

inputs.name: curiosity-questions
inputs.desc: The open questions that invite their story

inputs.name: acknowledgment-statements
inputs.desc: The sentences that show you understood their feelings

inputs.name: impact-statements
inputs.desc: The effect on you, free of intent claims

inputs.name: grounding-reframes
inputs.desc: The reframes that keep you steady under identity threat

outputs.name: conversation-opening
outputs.desc: An opening line that names the shared problem and invites their view before you deliver yours

outputs.name: proposed-next-steps
outputs.desc: A concrete, jointly framed proposal for what changes and how you both check it worked

process: Write an opening that states the purpose as a shared problem and signals you want to understand their view, not just state yours. 'I want to talk about the launch and understand how you saw it' opens, 'we need to talk about your mistakes' closes.
Sequence the middle: lead with a curiosity question, listen and acknowledge, then offer your impact. Delivering impact before listening tells them the outcome was decided before they spoke.
Draft next steps as a proposal, not a decree, and leave room for them to shape it. Ownership of the fix predicts whether the fix holds.
End by naming how you will both know it worked and when you will check. A next step with no check is a hope.

description: Diagnose which of the four listening failures you commit most, confirm it with real feedback, and practice the matching countermeasure for two weeks. The four failures are interrupting, rehearsing your reply, filtering for what you expected, and judging before understanding. You cannot fix all four at once, so find your dominant one and work it.

steps.description: Learn the four listening failures precisely enough to spot them in yourself. Interrupting cuts the speaker off. Rehearsing plans your reply while they talk. Filtering hears only what confirms your expectation. Judging decides they are wrong before they finish. Each feels like listening from the inside.

inputs.name: listening-context
inputs.desc: The settings where your listening matters most: one-on-ones, meetings, home, customer calls

inputs.name: recent-conversations
inputs.desc: Two or three recent conversations that did not go the way you wanted

outputs.name: failure-definitions
outputs.desc: The four failures written in your own words with a concrete example of each from your life

outputs.name: self-suspected-failures
outputs.desc: Your honest first guess at which one or two you commit most, before any feedback

process: Write each of the four failures in your own words. Generic definitions do not stick. Yours will.
For each failure, write one example from your recent conversations where you suspect you did it. If you cannot find an example, that failure is probably not your main one.
Rank the four by how often you suspect you commit each. This is a hypothesis, not a conclusion. Feedback comes next.
Note that the failure you least want to admit is often the one others see most. Flag that one for honest attention.

steps.description: Catch yourself in the act for one week. Self-report after the fact is unreliable, so log the moment as close to real time as you can. The goal is frequency data, not self-judgment.

inputs.name: failure-definitions
inputs.desc: The four failures in your own words

inputs.name: self-suspected-failures
inputs.desc: Your pre-feedback guess at your dominant failures

outputs.name: observation-log
outputs.desc: Dated entries noting which failure occurred, in what setting, and what triggered it

outputs.name: failure-frequency
outputs.desc: A count of each failure over the week, with the settings where each spiked

process: For one week, after each meaningful conversation, note any failure you caught yourself committing, the setting, and what set it off.
Record the trigger, not just the failure. Interrupting under time pressure and interrupting when excited call for different countermeasures.
Tally the counts at week's end. Look for the setting where your failures cluster, because that is where practice will pay off most.
Do not try to fix anything during this week. Observation changes behavior enough that early fixing contaminates the data.

steps.description: Ask two or three people who talk with you often which failure they see you commit. Others see your listening from the outside, where it actually lands. Ask a specific question, because a vague one gets a polite non-answer.

inputs.name: failure-definitions
inputs.desc: The four failures, to share so feedback is specific

inputs.name: self-suspected-failures
inputs.desc: Your guess, held back until after they answer so you do not lead them

outputs.name: external-feedback
outputs.desc: What each person reported, with any examples they offered

outputs.name: feedback-themes
outputs.desc: The failures that more than one person named, which carry more weight than a single report

process: Pick two or three people across different settings: a colleague, a family member, someone you manage or are managed by.
Ask the specific question: 'Of these four, which do you see me do most, and can you recall a time?' Share the four definitions so they answer in the same terms.
Do not reveal your own guess first, and do not defend yourself when they answer. A defense teaches them to stop being honest.
Note which failure more than one person named independently. Agreement across people is your strongest signal.

steps.description: Reconcile your self-observation with the outside feedback to name your one primary failure. When the two disagree, the outside view usually wins, because the failure you cannot see is the one doing the most damage.

inputs.name: failure-frequency
inputs.desc: Your self-logged counts over the week

inputs.name: external-feedback
inputs.desc: What others reported

inputs.name: feedback-themes
inputs.desc: The failures named by more than one person

outputs.name: primary-failure
outputs.desc: The single failure you will work on first, chosen from the combined evidence

outputs.name: evidence-summary
outputs.desc: The log counts and feedback that point to this failure, kept as a baseline to measure against later

process: Lay your self-counts beside the feedback themes. Where they agree, you have your answer.
Where they disagree, weight the outside view more heavily, especially for filtering and judging, which are nearly invisible from the inside.
Choose exactly one primary failure. Working two at once splits attention and neither improves.
Write the evidence summary as a baseline: the counts and the examples, so that in two weeks you can tell whether anything changed.

steps.description: Select the specific countermeasure for your primary failure. Each failure has a different fix, and a generic 'listen harder' fixes none of them. The countermeasure must be a small physical or mental action you can run in the moment.

inputs.name: primary-failure
inputs.desc: The single failure you will work on

outputs.name: countermeasure
outputs.desc: The specific in-the-moment action that counters your failure

outputs.name: practice-cues
outputs.desc: The signals that tell you the failure is about to happen, so you can trigger the countermeasure in time

process: Match the failure to its countermeasure. Interrupting: wait two full seconds of silence before you speak. Rehearsing: repeat the speaker's last phrase silently to keep your attention on them. Filtering: ask one question that could prove your expectation wrong. Judging: summarize their view to their satisfaction before you evaluate it.
Write the countermeasure as a single concrete action, not a principle. You will run it under pressure, so it has to be simple.
Identify the cues that precede your failure: a rising feeling, a pause you want to fill, a word that triggers your verdict. The cue is your trigger to run the countermeasure.
Choose one setting from your log to practice in first, ideally the one where the failure spiked.

steps.description: Build a two-week deliberate-practice plan with checkpoints. Two weeks is long enough to move a habit and short enough to stay focused. Practice needs a daily cue, a running count, and a midpoint check, or it quietly stops.

inputs.name: countermeasure
inputs.desc: The specific action you will practice

inputs.name: practice-cues
inputs.desc: The signals that trigger the countermeasure

inputs.name: evidence-summary
inputs.desc: The baseline counts to measure improvement against

outputs.name: practice-plan
outputs.desc: A two-week schedule naming where you practice daily and how you track each attempt

outputs.name: progress-checkpoints
outputs.desc: A midpoint and end check comparing new counts against the baseline, with a decision on what to do next

process: Name the daily setting where you will practice the countermeasure, so practice is scheduled rather than left to chance.
Track attempts with a simple count: times the cue appeared, times you ran the countermeasure. Running it is the win, even when the conversation is imperfect.
Set a day-seven checkpoint: compare the week's counts to the baseline, and adjust the cue if you keep missing it.
Set a day-fourteen check: if the failure dropped, lock the countermeasure in and pick your next failure. If it did not, keep the same failure and change the practice setting, not the target.

description: Run meetings that produce decisions. Every meeting names its decision in advance, states the options, and ships a pre-read 24 hours ahead. In the room: option advocacy, then objections, then the decision. At the end: what was decided, who owns what, by when. Minutes go out within the hour, while memory is still accurate.

steps.description: Name the single decision this meeting exists to make, phrased so it has a finite set of answers. A meeting called to 'discuss' a topic has no finish line and will not reach one. If you cannot name the decision, the meeting should be an email or should not happen.

inputs.name: meeting-request
inputs.desc: Why someone thinks a meeting is needed and the topic on the table

inputs.name: attendees
inputs.desc: Who would attend and the role each plays in the decision

outputs.name: decision-statement
outputs.desc: The decision to be made, written as a question with a bounded set of answers

outputs.name: decision-owner
outputs.desc: The one person accountable for making the call once the room has weighed in

process: Write the decision as a question: 'Do we ship on the first or delay two weeks?' not 'Let us talk about the timeline.'
Confirm the question has a finite answer set. If the answers are open-ended, narrow the question until they are not.
Name the single decision owner. A decision owned by the group is owned by no one and will reopen next week.
Run the necessity check: if the owner can decide with written input, cancel the meeting and collect the input in writing.

steps.description: Lay out the options under consideration, each with its trade-off in one line. A decision with one option is an announcement. Naming the real alternatives, including the option to do nothing, is what makes the meeting a decision rather than a rubber stamp.

inputs.name: decision-statement
inputs.desc: The decision to be made

outputs.name: options-set
outputs.desc: The two to four real options on the table, including the status-quo option where relevant

outputs.name: option-tradeoffs
outputs.desc: For each option, the gain and the cost stated in one line each

process: List the genuine options, capped at four. Beyond four, the meeting debates the list instead of the decision.
Include the do-nothing or status-quo option when it is real, so the room is comparing against the true alternative.
For each option, write the gain and the cost in one line each. An option with only gains listed is not being described honestly.
Cut any option that is a straw man placed only to make another look good. The room will see through it and trust the process less.

steps.description: Compose the pre-read and schedule it to land at least 24 hours before the meeting. The pre-read holds the decision, the options, the trade-offs, and your recommendation. The meeting is for disagreement, not for reading aloud what everyone could have read alone.

inputs.name: decision-statement
inputs.desc: The decision to be made

inputs.name: options-set
inputs.desc: The options on the table

inputs.name: option-tradeoffs
inputs.desc: The gain and cost for each option

outputs.name: preread-document
outputs.desc: A pre-read under two pages holding decision, options, trade-offs, and a recommendation

outputs.name: distribution-timing
outputs.desc: When the pre-read goes out and to whom, set at least 24 hours before the meeting

process: Write the pre-read to under two pages: decision and options first, trade-offs and recommendation second. Longer material goes in an appendix.
State a recommendation. A pre-read that lists options without a recommendation makes the author look neutral and leaves the room with nowhere to start.
Schedule distribution at least 24 hours ahead and label it as required reading for the meeting by name.
List who receives it. Anyone who will be asked to weigh in but does not get the pre-read will slow the room to their speed.

steps.description: Sequence the time in the room: brief advocacy for each option, then focused objections, then the decision. Advocacy before objections keeps the room from killing an option before it has been heard. A time box on each phase keeps the meeting from pooling in debate.

inputs.name: options-set
inputs.desc: The options to be advocated and challenged

inputs.name: decision-owner
inputs.desc: The person who will make the final call

outputs.name: meeting-agenda
outputs.desc: The in-room sequence: advocacy, objections, decision, with a purpose for each phase

outputs.name: timebox-plan
outputs.desc: Minutes allocated to each phase so the decision phase is never squeezed out

process: Open with brief advocacy: a short case for each option, ideally from someone who favors it, so every option gets a fair hearing.
Move to objections: invite disagreement with the recommendation and surface the risks. Silence here is treated as agreement, not as consent extracted by rushing.
Reserve a protected block for the decision itself. If objections run long, cut advocacy time, never the decision.
Set the time box per phase and name a facilitator to hold it, separate from the decision owner.

steps.description: Capture the decision live, in the room, before anyone leaves. State what was decided, who owns each action, and the date each is due, and read it back aloud. Memory starts editing the decision the moment the meeting ends, so capture beats recall.

inputs.name: meeting-agenda
inputs.desc: The sequence that led to the decision

inputs.name: decision-owner
inputs.desc: The person making the final call

outputs.name: decision-record
outputs.desc: What was decided, by whom, and with what caveats, confirmed aloud before anyone leaves

outputs.name: action-owners
outputs.desc: Each follow-up action with a single named owner and a due date

process: State the decision aloud and write it down as spoken: 'We decided to ship on the first. The owner is accountable for the release.'
Assign each action to one person. An action owned by a team is owned by no one.
Attach a due date to every action. An action with no date competes with everything else and loses.
Read the record back and ask for correction now. Confusion caught in the room is free. Confusion caught next week is expensive.

steps.description: Turn the decision record into minutes and send them within the hour. Minutes are the decision, the owners, and the dates, not a transcript of the discussion. Sent within the hour, they close the loop before anyone's memory diverges.

inputs.name: decision-record
inputs.desc: What was decided and confirmed in the room

inputs.name: action-owners
inputs.desc: The actions, owners, and due dates

outputs.name: meeting-minutes
outputs.desc: Short minutes stating the decision, the owners, and the dates, sent within one hour

outputs.name: dispatch-checklist
outputs.desc: Who receives the minutes, where they are stored, and when the first action check happens

process: Write the minutes as decision, owners, dates. Leave out the back-and-forth. People want to know what was decided, not who said what.
Send within one hour. The value of minutes decays fast, and a next-day send invites 'that is not what I agreed to.'
List recipients: everyone who was in the room plus anyone accountable for a downstream action.
Store the minutes where the next meeting can find them, and set the date of the first action check so follow-through is scheduled, not hoped for.

description: A system for written messages that get acted on. Put the action needed in the first sentence, then the minimum context. Structure for scanning with headers, bullets, and bold. One message, one topic. Number the actions. For a long document, write the executive summary as the document, because it is all that 80 percent of readers will read.

steps.description: Write the first sentence so it states the action needed and from whom. Readers decide in the first line whether to act, skim, or defer. A message that buries the ask under context gets filed, not done. Confirm the message carries one topic, not three.

inputs.name: message-purpose
inputs.desc: What you need to happen as a result of this message

inputs.name: recipient
inputs.desc: Who receives it and what they are able to decide or do

outputs.name: action-sentence
outputs.desc: A first sentence naming the action, the owner, and the deadline

outputs.name: single-topic-check
outputs.desc: A confirmation that the message holds one topic, with any extra topics split into separate messages

process: Write the first sentence as the action: 'Please approve the attached budget by Thursday' or 'No action needed, sharing for your awareness.'
Name who acts and by when inside that first sentence. A deadline that arrives three paragraphs later is a deadline most readers never reach.
If the message asks for two unrelated things, split it. One message, one topic, so the reader can act and archive in one pass.
If there is genuinely no action, say so in the first line, so the reader can file it with confidence instead of scanning for a hidden ask.

steps.description: Add only the context the reader needs to take the action, and no more. Writers include the context they needed to reach the conclusion. Readers need only the context required to act on it. The gap between those two is most of what makes messages too long.

inputs.name: action-sentence
inputs.desc: The action and deadline from the first sentence

inputs.name: single-topic-check
inputs.desc: Confirmation that the message is one topic

outputs.name: context-block
outputs.desc: The minimum context the reader needs to act, placed after the action

outputs.name: cut-context-log
outputs.desc: The background you removed, kept in case a reader asks or it belongs in a linked document

process: For each sentence of context, ask whether the reader can act without it. If yes, cut it.
Keep context that answers the questions the action raises: how much, by when, what happens if they say no.
Remove the story of how you got here. The reader cares about the conclusion and the ask, not your path to them.
Move cut context to a log or a linked document. Some of it belongs somewhere, just not in the body of this message.

steps.description: Structure the message so a reader can scan it in seconds. Headers, bullets, and bold let the eye find the action and the key facts without reading every word. A wall of text hides the ask inside it, and a hidden ask does not get done.

inputs.name: action-sentence
inputs.desc: The action to keep visible at the top

inputs.name: context-block
inputs.desc: The minimum context to lay out for scanning

outputs.name: scannable-layout
outputs.desc: The message arranged with headers, short bullets, and bold on the facts that drive the decision

outputs.name: formatting-rules
outputs.desc: The rules you applied, so your messages stay consistent and quick to scan over time

process: Keep the action sentence at the very top, before any header, so it is the first thing seen.
Break the context into short bullets. A bullet longer than two lines is a paragraph wearing a dot and should be split.
Bold only the few facts that drive the decision: the number, the date, the name. Bold everything and you have bolded nothing.
Add headers only if the message has distinct sections. A short message needs the action and a few bullets, not a table of contents.

steps.description: When the message asks for more than one action, number them and attach an owner and a deadline to each. A numbered list is easy to reply to point by point and hard to half-answer. Unnumbered asks buried in prose get partially done at best.

inputs.name: action-sentence
inputs.desc: The primary action from the first sentence

inputs.name: scannable-layout
inputs.desc: The scannable structure the actions will live in

outputs.name: numbered-actions
outputs.desc: Each requested action as a numbered item written as an imperative

outputs.name: owner-deadline-map
outputs.desc: For each numbered action, the single owner and the due date

process: Write each action as a numbered imperative: '1. Send the revised figures. 2. Confirm the vendor date.'
Attach one owner to each action. Two names on one action means neither will move first.
Attach a deadline to each action. Actions without dates sort to the bottom of everyone's list.
Keep the list short. More than five actions in one message is a project, and a project needs a plan, not an email.

steps.description: For a long document, write the executive summary as if it were the whole document, because for most readers it is. Around 80 percent will read only the summary and act on it. If the summary cannot stand alone, the document will be misread by the majority who never go past it.

inputs.name: scannable-layout
inputs.desc: The structured body the summary sits above

inputs.name: numbered-actions
inputs.desc: The actions the summary must carry so readers who stop here still act

outputs.name: executive-summary
outputs.desc: A summary that states the conclusion, the key facts, and the actions, readable on its own

outputs.name: summary-sufficiency-test
outputs.desc: The result of checking whether a reader who reads only the summary can act correctly

process: Write the summary to stand alone: the conclusion, the two or three facts behind it, and the actions required.
Put the actions in the summary, not only in the body. A reader who stops at the summary still needs to know what to do.
Run the sufficiency test: hand the summary alone to someone and ask what they would do. If they act correctly, the summary works.
Keep the body as the backup for the 20 percent who need the detail, and do not repeat the summary inside it.

steps.description: Run the final check before sending: one message, one topic, action visible, length earned. This last pass catches the message that drifted into a second subject or swelled past what the ask requires. The question is simple: can the reader act from the top without reading to the bottom?

inputs.name: executive-summary
inputs.desc: The stand-alone summary, if the piece is long

inputs.name: numbered-actions
inputs.desc: The actions the reader must take

inputs.name: summary-sufficiency-test
inputs.desc: Whether the summary alone was enough to act

outputs.name: final-message
outputs.desc: The message cleared to send, one topic, action first, no unearned length

outputs.name: send-readiness
outputs.desc: A short checklist result confirming topic, action placement, owners, and deadlines are all set

process: Confirm the message holds one topic. If a second topic crept in, split it into its own message now.
Confirm the reader can act from the first sentence or the summary alone, without hunting through the body.
Confirm every action has an owner and a date, and that no action hides in the prose instead of the list.
Read it once as the recipient. If any part makes you ask 'so what do you want from me,' fix that part, then send.

description: Structure a presentation with the Minto Pyramid: state the answer first, then the three supporting arguments, then the evidence under each. Your audience is there to be convinced, not confused, so lead with the conclusion. Each slide carries one idea, one visual, and one spoken explanation.

steps.description: Write the governing answer: the single sentence the whole presentation exists to deliver. In the Minto Pyramid, this answer sits at the top, and everything below supports it. Start here, because if the answer is not clear to you, no structure will make it clear to the audience.

inputs.name: presentation-goal
inputs.desc: What you want the audience to decide, do, or believe afterward

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who they are, what they already know, and what question they walked in with

outputs.name: governing-answer
outputs.desc: The one-sentence answer the presentation delivers, stated before any supporting detail

outputs.name: audience-question
outputs.desc: The question in the audience's mind that this answer resolves

process: Write the question the audience actually has: 'Should we enter this market?' or 'Why did the project slip?'
Write the answer to that question in one sentence. This is the governing answer, and it goes on the first content slide, not the last.
Check that the answer resolves the audience's question, not a different question you would rather answer.
Strip hedging from the answer. 'We should enter the market in the second half' is an answer. 'There are many factors to consider' is a stall.

steps.description: Build the three arguments that support the governing answer. Three is enough to be convincing and few enough to be remembered. The arguments should be distinct and together complete, so they cover the answer without overlapping each other.

inputs.name: governing-answer
inputs.desc: The answer the arguments must support

inputs.name: audience-question
inputs.desc: The question being resolved, to keep the arguments on point

outputs.name: supporting-arguments
outputs.desc: The three arguments that together justify the governing answer

outputs.name: mece-check
outputs.desc: A check that the arguments are distinct from each other and complete as a set

process: Ask what has to be true for the governing answer to hold. The answers to that are your arguments.
Reduce to three. If you have five, some are sub-points of others, so group them. If you have one, it is probably the answer restated, so break it down.
Check that the three do not overlap. Two arguments making the same point waste a slot and weaken the set.
Check that the three are complete: if the audience accepts all three, do they have to accept the answer? If not, an argument is missing.

steps.description: Map the evidence under each argument. Evidence is the bottom layer of the pyramid: the data, examples, and facts that make each argument believable. An argument without evidence is an assertion, and a presentation of assertions convinces no one who did not already agree.

inputs.name: supporting-arguments
inputs.desc: The three arguments that need evidence

outputs.name: evidence-map
outputs.desc: For each argument, the specific evidence that supports it

outputs.name: evidence-gaps
outputs.desc: Arguments that lack solid evidence, flagged for strengthening or softening before the dry run

process: For each argument, list the evidence you have: a number, a trend, a customer example, a precedent.
Rank the evidence by strength and keep the strongest one or two per argument. A slide of ten weak points is weaker than one strong one.
Flag arguments with thin or missing evidence. An argument you cannot support should be strengthened with new evidence or dropped.
Note where evidence is strong enough to lead the slide and where it only supports the spoken point.

steps.description: Decompose the content into slides, one idea per slide. Each slide carries a single idea, a single visual, and a single spoken explanation. The most common failure is a slide that holds three ideas, which forces the audience to read instead of listen and splits their attention from you.

inputs.name: supporting-arguments
inputs.desc: The arguments that become slide ideas

inputs.name: evidence-map
inputs.desc: The evidence that becomes the visual on each slide

outputs.name: slide-outline
outputs.desc: One slide per idea, each with its single visual and the spoken point it carries

outputs.name: slide-idea-count
outputs.desc: A count confirming no slide holds more than one idea, with overloaded slides split

process: Give each argument one lead slide, and give each strong piece of evidence its own slide if it needs room to land.
Write the one idea for each slide as a short sentence, and make it the slide's title. The title is the point, not a label like 'Results.'
Choose one visual per slide that shows the idea. If the visual needs a second visual to be understood, the slide holds two ideas.
Count ideas per slide. Any slide with more than one idea gets split, even if that grows the deck. More slides with one idea beat fewer slides with three.

steps.description: Sequence the slides into an answer-first storyline. The order mirrors the pyramid: governing answer, then the three arguments with their evidence, in the order that best carries the audience. Answer first means a listener who leaves early still got the point.

inputs.name: governing-answer
inputs.desc: The answer that opens the presentation

inputs.name: slide-outline
inputs.desc: The slides to sequence into a storyline

outputs.name: storyline-sequence
outputs.desc: The full slide order, opening on the answer and building through the three arguments

outputs.name: opening-slide
outputs.desc: The first content slide, carrying the governing answer so the point lands in the first minute

process: Open on the governing answer. Do not build up to it over ten slides. State it, then support it.
Order the three arguments for the audience, usually strongest first for a skeptical room and most familiar first for a cautious one.
Place each argument's evidence directly after it, so the support arrives while the claim is fresh.
End by returning to the answer and the action it implies. The close restates the top of the pyramid, now earned.

steps.description: Run the presentation once out loud and tighten it. The dry run reveals the slides that confuse, the transitions that stall, and the places where you talk past your own point. A slide that you cannot explain in one or two spoken sentences is a slide that holds too much.

inputs.name: storyline-sequence
inputs.desc: The sequenced slides to run through

inputs.name: evidence-gaps
inputs.desc: The weak-evidence points flagged earlier, to confirm they were fixed or cut

outputs.name: tightened-deck
outputs.desc: The deck after the dry run: confusing slides fixed, weak slides cut, transitions smoothed

outputs.name: dry-run-notes
outputs.desc: Where the run lost clarity or stalled, and what changed as a result

process: Present the whole thing aloud to one listener or to a recording. Note every slide where you hesitate or over-explain.
For each slide, confirm you can state its one idea in one or two spoken sentences. If you cannot, the slide holds too much, so split or cut it.
Confirm the evidence gaps flagged earlier were closed. Any argument still thin should be strengthened or dropped now, not in the room.
Check the transitions. If moving between two slides needs a long bridge, their order is wrong or one of them is unnecessary.

description: Prepare for a negotiation before you are in the room. Define your BATNA and estimate theirs, because a weak BATNA means less power and should be improved first. Set your reservation price and your target, open more ambitiously than your target, and prepare three things that cost you little but are worth a lot to them.

steps.description: Define your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement, and estimate theirs. Your BATNA is what you do if this deal falls through, and it sets the floor on what you should accept. Knowing both BATNAs tells you who holds the leverage before a word is spoken.

inputs.name: negotiation-context
inputs.desc: What is being negotiated, with whom, and what each side wants from it

inputs.name: counterparty
inputs.desc: Who the other side is and what you know about their situation and constraints

outputs.name: your-batna
outputs.desc: Your best alternative if no agreement is reached, stated concretely

outputs.name: their-batna-estimate
outputs.desc: Your best estimate of the other side's alternative, with the evidence behind the estimate

process: Write your BATNA as a concrete action, not a feeling: 'If we do not agree, we sign with the other vendor at their quoted rate.'
Estimate their BATNA from what you know of their options, their timeline, and their pressures. Guessing is fine as long as you mark it as a guess.
Compare the two. The side with the stronger BATNA walks in with more leverage, and knowing which side that is changes how you play.
If you cannot name your own BATNA, you are negotiating blind and will accept a bad deal out of fear of no deal.

steps.description: If your BATNA is weak, improve it before you negotiate rather than during. The strength of your BATNA, not your arguments in the room, is the real source of your leverage. A better alternative, even a modest one, changes the whole negotiation more than any clever tactic.

inputs.name: your-batna
inputs.desc: Your current best alternative

inputs.name: their-batna-estimate
inputs.desc: The other side's estimated alternative, for comparison

outputs.name: batna-strength-rating
outputs.desc: A rating of how strong your BATNA is relative to theirs: strong, even, or weak

outputs.name: batna-improvement-actions
outputs.desc: Concrete actions to strengthen your alternative before entering the negotiation

process: Rate your BATNA against theirs: strong if you can walk away comfortably, weak if walking away hurts you more than them.
If it is weak, list ways to improve it: line up a second option, extend your timeline, reduce your dependence on this deal.
Take the improvement actions before the negotiation where you can. A real alternative secured in advance beats a bluff in the room.
If the BATNA cannot be improved in time, plan to protect it: keep it private, and do not signal how much you need the deal.

steps.description: Set two numbers: your reservation price and your target. The reservation price is the worst deal you will accept, anchored to your BATNA. The target is the outcome you are aiming for, set at the ambitious edge of what is realistic. Both are decided in advance, in the calm before the room.

inputs.name: your-batna
inputs.desc: Your alternative, which anchors the reservation price

inputs.name: batna-strength-rating
inputs.desc: How much leverage you hold, which shapes how ambitious the target can be

outputs.name: reservation-price
outputs.desc: The least favorable terms you will accept before walking to your BATNA

outputs.name: target-price
outputs.desc: The outcome you are aiming for, set at the ambitious end of realistic

process: Set the reservation price just better than your BATNA. Accepting worse than your BATNA means you should have walked.
Set the target at the ambitious edge of what the facts support. Negotiators who set modest targets reach modest outcomes.
Write both numbers down before the negotiation. Deciding them in the room, under pressure, is how people talk themselves into bad deals.
Let the strength rating calibrate the target: strong leverage supports a more ambitious target, weak leverage pulls it toward realism.

steps.description: Build an opening position more ambitious than your target but still defensible. The opening anchors the negotiation, and a credible, ambitious anchor pulls the final outcome toward you. Ambitious without justification reads as a bluff, so pair the number with a reason.

inputs.name: target-price
inputs.desc: The outcome you are aiming for, which the opening sits above

inputs.name: their-batna-estimate
inputs.desc: Their alternative, so the opening is ambitious without pushing them to walk

outputs.name: opening-position
outputs.desc: The first offer you will make, set above your target and anchored with a rationale

outputs.name: opening-justification
outputs.desc: The reason that makes the opening credible rather than a bluff

process: Set the opening above your target so there is room to concede toward the target and still land well.
Keep the opening defensible. An anchor the other side can laugh off does not anchor anything and costs you credibility.
Write the justification that comes with the opening: the comparable, the cost basis, the value delivered. The reason is what makes the number stick.
Check the opening against their BATNA. If it is so aggressive that walking to their alternative looks better, soften it until it does not.

steps.description: Inventory three things you can offer that cost you little but are worth a lot to them, and anticipate the same in reverse. These asymmetric trades are where value is created rather than just divided. The best agreements trade on differences in what each side values.

inputs.name: negotiation-context
inputs.desc: What is being negotiated and the full set of terms in play

inputs.name: their-batna-estimate
inputs.desc: Their situation and pressures, which reveal what they value most

outputs.name: low-cost-high-value-offers
outputs.desc: Three things you can give that cost you little and are worth a lot to the other side

outputs.name: their-likely-asks
outputs.desc: The concessions they are likely to want, and which of them cost you little to grant

process: List every term beyond price: timing, volume, exclusivity, payment schedule, scope, support. Value lives in these, not only in the headline number.
Find three you can give cheaply that they would value highly. Faster payment, a reference, a longer term, flexibility on a date they care about.
Anticipate their asks and sort them by what each would cost you. Cheap-to-you asks are concessions you can grant freely to win something back.
Pair your low-cost offers with the asks you most want, so each thing you give is traded, not donated.

steps.description: Plan the concession sequence from your opening down toward your reservation price, trading the low-cost items along the way. Concessions given without a trade train the other side to keep pushing. A planned ladder keeps you from conceding too fast or past your floor.

inputs.name: opening-position
inputs.desc: Where you start

inputs.name: reservation-price
inputs.desc: The floor you will not cross

inputs.name: low-cost-high-value-offers
inputs.desc: The items you trade on the way down

outputs.name: concession-ladder
outputs.desc: The planned sequence of concessions from opening toward reservation, each tied to something you get back

outputs.name: walk-away-triggers
outputs.desc: The conditions under which you stop and go to your BATNA instead of conceding further

process: Plan concessions as decreasing steps. Large early concessions signal there is far more room, so shrink each step as you approach your floor.
Attach a trade to each concession. 'I can move on the date if you move on volume.' A concession for nothing invites the next demand.
Mark the reservation price as a hard stop. Below it, your BATNA is the better deal, so you walk.
Write the walk-away triggers plainly, so that under pressure you recognize the moment to stop rather than rationalize one more concession.

description: Turn a message into a story so it is remembered and acted on. Use the four-part structure of protagonist, problem, struggle, and resolution. Facts delivered inside a story are far more memorable than facts delivered alone, a result Jerome Bruner put at roughly twenty times. Story is not decoration on the message, it is how people process and retain it.

steps.description: Extract the one message the story has to carry and the change you want it to produce. A story with two messages lands neither. Decide the single idea first, because every later choice of protagonist, problem, and resolution is made in service of it.

inputs.name: influence-goal
inputs.desc: What you want the audience to believe, feel, or do after the story

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who the audience is and what they currently think about the topic

outputs.name: core-message
outputs.desc: The single idea the story must deliver, in one sentence

outputs.name: change-sought
outputs.desc: The specific shift in belief or action the story is meant to produce

process: Write the one idea the story must leave behind. If you list two, choose the one the other depends on.
Write the change you want: what the audience thinks or does differently once the story lands.
Check that the idea is a message, not a topic. 'Customer trust is fragile' is a message. 'Our support process' is a topic.
Keep this core message in view through every later step. Anything in the story that does not serve it is a candidate to cut.

steps.description: Choose a protagonist the audience can identify with. The audience experiences the story through the protagonist, so the protagonist has to be someone they recognize or can stand in for. A hero too distant from the audience turns the story into someone else's problem.

inputs.name: core-message
inputs.desc: The idea the story carries

inputs.name: change-sought
inputs.desc: The shift the story aims to produce

outputs.name: protagonist
outputs.desc: The central figure of the story, chosen so the audience identifies with them

outputs.name: audience-identification-note
outputs.desc: Why this protagonist connects to the audience and where the connection might be weak

process: Pick a protagonist close to the audience: a customer like them, a team like theirs, a person in their role.
Make the protagonist specific, not a category. 'A warehouse manager named in the story' lands harder than 'operations teams.'
Check the identification. If the audience would see the protagonist as other, the story's lesson will feel like it applies to someone else.
Confirm the protagonist can plausibly face the problem that carries your core message. The right hero for one message is the wrong hero for another.

steps.description: Define the problem the protagonist faces and the stakes if it goes unsolved. The problem is the engine of the story, and the stakes are why anyone keeps listening. A problem with no real stakes produces a story with no tension, which the audience forgets as fast as a plain fact.

inputs.name: protagonist
inputs.desc: The central figure who faces the problem

inputs.name: core-message
inputs.desc: The idea the problem must set up

outputs.name: problem-statement
outputs.desc: The concrete problem the protagonist faces, framed to set up the core message

outputs.name: stakes
outputs.desc: What the protagonist stands to lose if the problem is not solved

process: State the problem concretely, as the protagonist would feel it, not as an abstract issue.
Name the stakes: what breaks, what is lost, what changes for the worse if the problem wins.
Tie the problem to the core message. The way the protagonist escapes this problem is what proves your point.
Keep the stakes real and proportionate. Overstated stakes read as manipulation and cost you the audience's trust.

steps.description: Build the struggle, the believable middle where the protagonist works toward a resolution and it is not easy. The struggle is where memory and emotion attach, because a problem solved instantly teaches nothing and moves no one. A false step before the turning point makes the resolution earned rather than given.

inputs.name: problem-statement
inputs.desc: The problem that drives the struggle

inputs.name: protagonist
inputs.desc: The figure working through the struggle

outputs.name: struggle-arc
outputs.desc: The sequence of attempts, setbacks, and effort between the problem and the resolution

outputs.name: turning-point
outputs.desc: The moment the struggle shifts toward resolution, which carries the core message

process: Lay out the attempts the protagonist makes, including one that does not work. Struggle without a setback is not struggle.
Place a turning point where something changes: a realization, a new approach, outside help. This moment is where your core message lives.
Keep the struggle believable for this protagonist and this problem. An unrealistic struggle breaks the identification you built.
Make the turning point grow out of the protagonist's effort, so the resolution feels earned and the lesson feels true.

steps.description: Write the resolution and map it back to the core message so the point lands without a lecture. The resolution shows how the struggle ends, and a well-built story lets the audience draw the message themselves. Stating the moral too bluntly after a strong story insults the audience and weakens the effect.

inputs.name: struggle-arc
inputs.desc: The attempts and setbacks leading to the resolution

inputs.name: turning-point
inputs.desc: The shift that made resolution possible

inputs.name: core-message
inputs.desc: The idea the resolution must deliver

outputs.name: resolution
outputs.desc: How the protagonist's problem is resolved, shown rather than summarized

outputs.name: message-landing
outputs.desc: How the resolution connects to the core message, with the right amount said aloud

process: Write the resolution as an outcome shown through what the protagonist does and gains, not as a summary.
Connect the resolution to the core message. The way the problem was solved should be the proof of your idea.
Decide how much to state outright. If the story carries the message well, one short line at the end is enough. If the link is subtle, say slightly more.
Check that the resolution delivers the change you sought. If the audience would finish the story and still not shift, the resolution is not aimed at the message.

steps.description: Package the full arc with delivery notes and a memorability check. The same story told flat and told well land differently, so the delivery choices matter as much as the structure. The final check is whether a listener could retell the story a day later and carry the message with it.

inputs.name: protagonist
inputs.desc: The central figure

inputs.name: problem-statement
inputs.desc: The problem that opens the story

inputs.name: struggle-arc
inputs.desc: The believable middle

inputs.name: resolution
inputs.desc: How it ends and what it means

outputs.name: story-script
outputs.desc: The full story from protagonist to resolution, sequenced and ready to tell

outputs.name: memorability-check
outputs.desc: The result of testing whether a listener can retell the story and recover the core message

process: Assemble the full arc in order: protagonist, problem and stakes, struggle and turning point, resolution and message.
Add delivery notes: where to slow down, where the detail is vivid, where to let a pause carry weight.
Cut anything that does not serve the core message. A tight story is remembered. A sprawling one is lost.
Run the memorability check: tell it to one person, wait, and ask them to retell it. If the message survives their retelling, the story works.

description: Decline a request cleanly without burning the relationship. Acknowledge the request, state the no clearly, give one brief real reason rather than an excuse, and offer an alternative if a real one exists. One apology is polite, three is submissive. Saying yes when you mean no usually costs more social capital than the honest no would have.

steps.description: Assess the request and the true cost of saying yes. Most reflexive yeses happen because the cost is not counted until later. Count it now: the hours, the trade-offs against other commitments, and the resentment a grudging yes tends to breed.

inputs.name: request-received
inputs.desc: What is being asked of you and by when

inputs.name: relationship-context
inputs.desc: Who is asking, your relationship, and what is at stake between you

outputs.name: request-summary
outputs.desc: The request stated plainly, including what a yes would actually commit you to

outputs.name: cost-of-yes
outputs.desc: The real cost of agreeing: time, trade-offs against other commitments, and likely resentment

process: Restate the request in full, including the parts left implicit. 'Can you help with the launch' often means weeks, not an afternoon.
Count the direct cost in time and the indirect cost in what you would give up to say yes.
Note the resentment cost. A yes you will resent damages the relationship more slowly but more deeply than a clean no.
Separate the request from the relationship. You can value the person and still decline the request.

steps.description: Decide whether this is a real no by weighing the cost of yes against the social cost of the no. The point is not to decline everything, it is to decline what you should. Compare honestly, because the hidden cost of a dishonest yes is almost always higher than it first appears.

inputs.name: cost-of-yes
inputs.desc: The real cost of agreeing

inputs.name: request-summary
inputs.desc: The request and what it commits you to

outputs.name: no-decision
outputs.desc: Whether this is a no, a yes, or a conditional yes, with the reasoning

outputs.name: decision-rationale
outputs.desc: The real reason behind the decision, which becomes the honest basis for the message

process: Weigh the cost of yes against the social cost of a clear no. The social cost of a no is usually smaller and shorter than people fear.
Recall what a dishonest yes costs: the missed deadline, the half-effort, the trust lost when you cannot deliver. That is the true comparison.
Decide: no, yes, or a conditional yes that trims the request to something you can give fully.
Write the real reason for the decision. This is for you now, and it becomes the honest basis for the brief reason you will give.

steps.description: Write the acknowledgment that opens the message. Acknowledging the request shows you took it seriously and respects the person before you decline. A no that opens with the refusal, skipping acknowledgment, reads as dismissive even when it is not.

inputs.name: request-summary
inputs.desc: The request to acknowledge accurately

outputs.name: acknowledgment-line
outputs.desc: An opening that shows you understood the request and took it seriously

outputs.name: tone-note
outputs.desc: The tone to carry through, matched to the relationship and the ask

process: Open by naming the request accurately, so the person sees you understood what they asked.
Show it mattered without implying a yes. 'Thank you for thinking of me for this' acknowledges without committing.
Keep the acknowledgment short. A long preamble reads as softening the ground for a no the person can already feel coming.
Set the tone to fit the relationship: warmer for a friend, plainer for a transactional ask. The tone carries through the whole message.

steps.description: State the no clearly and give one brief real reason, not an excuse. A vague no invites a second ask and a negotiation. A clear no with a genuine reason closes the matter and keeps your credibility. An excuse, by contrast, is a reason you do not believe, and people can tell.

inputs.name: no-decision
inputs.desc: The decision to decline

inputs.name: decision-rationale
inputs.desc: The real reason behind the decision

outputs.name: no-statement
outputs.desc: A clear, unambiguous no that does not leave the door half open

outputs.name: brief-reason
outputs.desc: One short, true reason, offered without over-explaining or inventing an excuse

process: State the no plainly: 'I am not able to take this on.' Avoid phrasing that reads as a maybe unless you mean maybe.
Give one real reason drawn from your rationale, in a sentence. The truth, briefly stated, closes the matter.
Do not stack reasons. Multiple reasons invite the person to solve each one and reopen the ask.
Do not invent an excuse. An excuse is a reason you would drop if challenged, and offering one teaches the person to challenge it.

steps.description: Offer an alternative only if a real one exists. A genuine alternative softens the no and keeps the relationship productive. A hollow alternative offered to feel helpful creates a new obligation you did not intend and a new thing to decline later.

inputs.name: request-summary
inputs.desc: The request, to find an alternative that addresses the underlying need

inputs.name: cost-of-yes
inputs.desc: The cost that ruled out the full yes, to keep the alternative within what you can give

outputs.name: alternative-offer
outputs.desc: A real alternative you can deliver: a smaller slice, a different time, another person, a useful pointer

outputs.name: no-alternative-note
outputs.desc: If no honest alternative exists, a note to that effect so you do not invent a hollow one

process: Ask what the person actually needs under the request. An alternative that meets the need, even partly, is worth more than the full yes you declined.
Offer only what you can deliver: a smaller piece, a later date, a referral to someone better placed, a resource that helps.
Keep the alternative within the cost you can bear, or you have just said yes to a different thing you will resent.
If there is no real alternative, say nothing more. A hollow offer is worse than none, because it reopens the ask.

steps.description: Assemble the full message with one apology at most and no over-explaining. The parts are acknowledgment, clear no, brief reason, and alternative if real. The final pass removes the extra apologies and the nervous padding that turn a respectful no into a plea for permission.

inputs.name: acknowledgment-line
inputs.desc: The opening that shows you took the request seriously

inputs.name: no-statement
inputs.desc: The clear no

inputs.name: brief-reason
inputs.desc: The one short real reason

inputs.name: alternative-offer
inputs.desc: The real alternative, or the note that there is none

outputs.name: final-no-message
outputs.desc: The assembled message: acknowledgment, no, reason, and alternative where real

outputs.name: apology-count-check
outputs.desc: A check confirming at most one apology and no padding that undercuts the no

process: Assemble in order: acknowledgment, no, brief reason, alternative if one is real.
Count the apologies. One 'I am sorry' is courteous. Three signals you think you owe a debt for declining, which invites pushback.
Cut the padding: 'I really hope this is okay,' 'please do not be upset,' 'I feel terrible.' These ask the person to reassure you and reopen the matter.
Read it once. If it still sounds like you are asking permission to say no, trim until it sounds like a decision stated with respect.

description: Communicate upward so your manager can act. Know what they care about and frame your message in their terms. Lead with the headline, then state specifically what you need. For bad news, go early, say what you are doing about it, and say what you need. Never let your boss be surprised in front of others.

steps.description: Map what your manager actually cares about and the pressures they are under. Upward communication fails most often when a message is framed around what you care about instead of what they do. Their priorities, their metrics, and the people they answer to are the frame your message has to fit.

inputs.name: manager-context
inputs.desc: Your manager's goals, the metrics they are measured on, and who they report to

inputs.name: topic
inputs.desc: The thing you need to communicate upward

outputs.name: manager-priorities
outputs.desc: What your manager cares about most right now, ranked

outputs.name: decision-pressures
outputs.desc: The pressures and constraints shaping how they will receive your message

process: List what your manager is measured on and what they talk about most. Those are their priorities, whatever the org chart says.
Identify who they answer to and what those people expect. Your manager's boss is often the real audience behind your message.
Note current pressures: a deadline, a budget review, a problem they are already fighting. Your message lands into that context.
Rank the priorities so you know which one to connect your topic to. The top priority is the frame.

steps.description: Translate your topic into your manager's terms. The same fact can be framed as a technical detail or as a risk to a goal they own. Framed in their terms, your message connects to something they already care about, and it earns attention instead of competing for it.

inputs.name: manager-priorities
inputs.desc: What the manager cares about most

inputs.name: topic
inputs.desc: The thing you need to communicate

outputs.name: reframed-topic
outputs.desc: Your topic restated in terms of the manager's priorities and goals

outputs.name: their-language-map
outputs.desc: The words and metrics your manager uses, to replace your internal terms

process: Connect your topic to the top priority it touches. A migration delay becomes a risk to the launch date the manager owns.
Translate internal terms into the manager's language. Replace the system name with the outcome it affects.
Lead with the effect on their goal, not the mechanism. They need the mechanism only if they ask.
Check the frame against their pressures. A message framed around last quarter's priority lands on a manager who has moved on.

steps.description: Write the headline and lead with it. Managers process many inputs a day and read the first line to decide how much attention the rest deserves. A headline that states the point up front gets the message read. A message that builds to its point gets skimmed and misfiled.

inputs.name: reframed-topic
inputs.desc: The topic framed in the manager's terms

outputs.name: headline
outputs.desc: The one-line headline that states the point before any detail

outputs.name: one-line-why-it-matters
outputs.desc: A single line connecting the headline to the priority it affects

process: Write the headline as the point itself: 'The vendor will miss the date, and here is the plan.' Not 'An update on the vendor.'
Keep it to one line. A headline that runs to three sentences is a paragraph, and the reader has already started skimming.
Add one line on why it matters, tied to the priority it affects, so the manager knows why to keep reading.
Put the headline first, before any background. Background before the headline is the most common way an upward message loses its reader.

steps.description: State specifically what you need from your manager, and whether this is a decision or an awareness item. A vague ask leaves the manager guessing at their role and often produces nothing. Marking a message as decision-needed or awareness-only lets them triage it correctly.

inputs.name: headline
inputs.desc: The point the ask follows from

inputs.name: manager-priorities
inputs.desc: What the manager cares about, to frame the ask in their interest

outputs.name: specific-ask
outputs.desc: Exactly what you need: a decision, an approval, an introduction, or nothing but awareness

outputs.name: decision-or-fyi-flag
outputs.desc: A clear marker of whether this needs a decision or is for awareness only

process: State the ask as a specific action: 'I need your approval on the revised budget by Friday' or 'I need you to raise this with the vendor's executive.'
If no action is needed, say so plainly, so the manager can note it and move on instead of hunting for a hidden ask.
Flag the message as decision-needed or awareness-only at the top. This single marker is what lets a busy manager triage correctly.
Make the ask proportionate. Asking the manager to do what you could do yourself spends credibility you will want later.

steps.description: When the message is bad news, structure it to go early, lead with what you are already doing about it, and state what you need. Managers can handle bad news, but not late bad news, and not bad news with no plan attached. Early plus a plan turns a problem into a managed situation.

inputs.name: topic
inputs.desc: The situation, including whether it is bad news

inputs.name: specific-ask
inputs.desc: What you need, which bad news usually includes

outputs.name: bad-news-structure
outputs.desc: The bad news framed as what happened, what you are doing, and what you need, in that order

outputs.name: timing-plan
outputs.desc: When to deliver it, chosen to be as early as the facts allow

process: Lead with the news and the action you have already taken. 'The build failed, and I have rolled back and started the fix' is a managed problem.
State what you need from the manager next, if anything, so the message ends on a path forward.
Go early. Bad news delivered late costs trust twice: once for the problem and once for the delay in surfacing it.
Do not pad bad news with reassurance it cannot support. State the facts, the plan, and the ask, and let the plan do the reassuring.

steps.description: Assemble the message and make sure your manager is never surprised in front of others. A manager caught off guard in a meeting by something you knew will remember it. A short pre-brief before anything goes public protects them and protects your standing with them.

inputs.name: headline
inputs.desc: The leading point

inputs.name: specific-ask
inputs.desc: What you need and whether it is a decision

inputs.name: bad-news-structure
inputs.desc: The bad-news framing, if the message carries bad news

inputs.name: timing-plan
inputs.desc: When the message goes out

outputs.name: upward-message
outputs.desc: The assembled message: headline, framed detail, specific ask, delivered on the timing plan

outputs.name: pre-brief-plan
outputs.desc: A plan to brief the manager before anything that could surprise them in front of others

process: Assemble in order: headline, the detail framed in their terms, the specific ask with its decision-or-awareness flag.
Identify anything in the message that could reach a group setting: a status meeting, a leadership review, a board update.
Pre-brief the manager on those items before the public moment, even in a sentence. The goal is that nothing you knew surprises them in a room.
Confirm the timing. Early and privately first, then public, so the manager is never learning it at the same time as their peers.

description: Communicate across cultures using Erin Meyer's Culture Map. The map sets out eight dimensions on which cultures predictably differ. Identify where you and your counterpart sit on the dimensions that matter for this interaction, then adjust to the listener's expectations. Across cultures, the communicator who adapts is the effective one.

steps.description: Learn the eight dimensions of the Culture Map well enough to place a conversation on them. The dimensions cover how people communicate, give negative feedback, persuade, lead, decide, build trust, disagree, and treat time. Each is a spectrum, and cultures sit at different points, not at a right answer.

inputs.name: communication-setting
inputs.desc: The interaction you are preparing for: a negotiation, a team you lead, a client relationship

inputs.name: counterpart-culture
inputs.desc: The cultural background of the people you are communicating with

outputs.name: dimension-definitions
outputs.desc: The eight dimensions defined as spectrums, each with its two poles described plainly

outputs.name: setting-summary
outputs.desc: A short summary of the interaction and which dimensions are likely to matter most in it

process: Write the eight dimensions as spectrums: communicating from low-context to high-context, evaluating from direct to indirect negative feedback, persuading from principles-first to applications-first, leading from egalitarian to hierarchical, deciding from consensual to top-down, trusting from task-based to relationship-based, disagreeing from confrontational to confrontation-avoiding, and scheduling from linear time to flexible time.
For each dimension, describe both poles in plain terms so you can recognize them in behavior, not just name them.
Summarize the interaction you are preparing for, and flag which dimensions are most likely to shape it. A negotiation leans on trusting and disagreeing, a project handoff on scheduling and deciding.
Remember the dimensions are relative. A culture is direct or indirect only compared with another, so the comparison is what matters, not the label.

steps.description: Plot your own position on each dimension. You cannot see a gap until you have located yourself, and most people mistake their own cultural defaults for simply the normal way to communicate. Naming your own position turns an invisible default into one point on a spectrum.

inputs.name: dimension-definitions
inputs.desc: The eight dimensions as spectrums

outputs.name: your-positions
outputs.desc: Your own position on each of the eight dimensions, with a note on how strongly you hold it

outputs.name: your-defaults-note
outputs.desc: The habits you treat as simply normal, which are in fact one cultural position among several

process: Place yourself on each dimension based on how you actually behave, not how you would like to.
Note where you hold a position strongly. A strong default is the one most likely to cause friction when the counterpart sits at the other pole.
Name the behaviors you consider simply normal: how blunt your feedback is, how you show respect to seniority, how you treat a start time.
Recognize these as a position, not a standard. The counterpart has their own normal, equally invisible to them.

steps.description: Plot your counterpart's likely position on each dimension, using evidence and holding the estimate loosely. Culture predicts tendencies, not individuals, so a national pattern is a starting hypothesis to be corrected by what the actual person does. The aim is a working estimate, not a stereotype.

inputs.name: dimension-definitions
inputs.desc: The eight dimensions as spectrums

inputs.name: setting-summary
inputs.desc: The interaction and the dimensions most likely to matter

outputs.name: counterpart-positions
outputs.desc: The counterpart's estimated position on each dimension that matters for this interaction

outputs.name: evidence-caveats
outputs.desc: Where the estimate is weak and where the individual may differ from the cultural pattern

process: Estimate the counterpart's position on each relevant dimension from cultural patterns and from anything you have observed directly.
Weight observed behavior over general pattern. An individual who has worked across cultures may sit far from their national default.
Mark the estimates you are least sure of, so you watch for evidence that corrects them early in the interaction.
Hold the estimate as a hypothesis. Treating a cultural tendency as a certain fact about a person is the error the map is meant to prevent.

steps.description: Identify the dimensions where you and your counterpart sit far apart and where that gap will do the most damage. Not every difference matters for every interaction. The gaps worth preparing for are the ones that intersect with what this specific conversation depends on.

inputs.name: your-positions
inputs.desc: Your positions on the eight dimensions

inputs.name: counterpart-positions
inputs.desc: The counterpart's estimated positions

outputs.name: key-gaps
outputs.desc: The dimensions where you and the counterpart sit far apart and the gap matters for this interaction

outputs.name: gap-risk-ranking
outputs.desc: The gaps ranked by how much damage a mismatch would do in this specific setting

process: Lay your positions beside the counterpart's and measure the distance on each dimension.
Keep the gaps that intersect with what this interaction depends on. A trust-dimension gap matters more for a new partnership than for a one-time transaction.
Rank the surviving gaps by the damage a mismatch would cause: a blown relationship, a misread yes, a deadline understood differently.
Focus on the top two or three. Trying to adjust for all eight at once produces stilted, unnatural communication that helps no one.

steps.description: For each key gap, plan the specific adjustment to the listener's expectations and note how not to misread them. Adaptation runs both ways: you change how you send, and you reinterpret how you receive. A direct message from an indirect culture carries more weight than its plain words show.

inputs.name: key-gaps
inputs.desc: The dimensions where the gap matters most

inputs.name: gap-risk-ranking
inputs.desc: The gaps ranked by potential damage

outputs.name: adjustment-actions
outputs.desc: For each key gap, the specific change in how you send your message

outputs.name: do-not-misread-notes
outputs.desc: For each key gap, how to correctly interpret what the counterpart sends given their position

process: For each gap, write the specific adjustment to how you communicate. Facing an indirect-feedback culture, soften criticism and read a mild word as a strong signal.
Write the matching interpretation note. A yes from a confrontation-avoiding, high-context counterpart may mean 'I hear you,' not 'I agree.'
Adjust toward the listener's expectations, since across cultures the burden of adapting falls on the communicator who wants to be understood.
Keep adjustments to the top gaps so your communication stays natural. Overcorrecting on every dimension reads as awkward and can give offense of its own.

steps.description: Rehearse the specific upcoming interaction with the adjustments in place, and prepare check-back questions that catch a misread before it costs anything. Rehearsal turns a list of adjustments into something you can actually do under the pressure of a live conversation. A check-back question verifies understanding without forcing the counterpart to contradict you.

inputs.name: adjustment-actions
inputs.desc: The specific changes to how you send your message

inputs.name: setting-summary
inputs.desc: The interaction being prepared for

outputs.name: interaction-plan
outputs.desc: The upcoming interaction scripted with the adjustments applied at the moments they matter

outputs.name: check-back-questions
outputs.desc: Questions that confirm understanding across the gap without forcing an open contradiction

process: Walk through the interaction applying each adjustment at the moment it matters: the opening, the ask, the feedback, the close.
Prepare check-back questions that surface a misread safely. 'What are the next steps as you see them' reveals a different understanding without a confrontation.
Plan for the gaps you are least sure of by watching for the behaviors that would confirm or correct your estimate early.
Keep the plan flexible. The map prepares you to read the person in front of you, and the live evidence overrides the estimate every time.
